title: Romance of the Three Kingdoms
subtitle: The endless Yangtze rolls eastward · Its waves wash away all heroes
description: Romance of the Three Kingdoms is China's first full-length historical novel in chapter form, written by Luo Guanzhong in the late Yuan and early Ming dynasties. It portrays nearly a century of historical upheaval from the end of the Eastern Han to the beginning of the Western Jin. The book opens with the Peach Garden Oath of Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei, and ends with the reunification of the empire under the Jin Dynasty, creating immortal characters such as Zhuge Liang, Cao Cao, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei. It is hailed as one of the Four Great Classical Novels of Chinese literature.

route.title: Romance of the Three Kingdoms: The Epic Road of Golden Spears and Iron Horses, Where Heroes Were Born
route.intro:
The endless Yangtze rolls eastward, its waves washing away all heroes. Right and wrong, success and failure — all turn to nothing in a flash. The green hills remain forever, greeting sunset after sunset.
Luo Guanzhong, style name Ben, literary name Lake-and-Sea Recluse, was a native of Taiyuan (or some say Dongyuan) in the late Yuan and early Ming dynasties. Born in an age of chaos, he witnessed firsthand the blood-soaked struggle among contending powers and the dynastic transition of the late Yuan. He poured his life's experience and profound historical reflection into this seven-hundred-and-fifty-thousand-character masterpiece. The book's grand sweep captures the loyalty, wisdom, courage, success, and ruin of a host of heroes. Let us follow in the footsteps of the heroes of the Three Kingdoms — from the Peach Garden in Zhuo Commandery to the Temple of Marquis Wu in Chengdu, from the flames of Red Cliffs to the autumn wind on Wuzhang Plains — traversing eighteen centuries to visit the nationally protected cultural heritage sites that bear witness to golden spears, iron horses, loyal hearts, and righteous courage.

stops.title: Stop One: Zhuo Commandery's Peach Garden · A Bond of Life and Death
stops.content: In the closing years of the Eastern Han dynasty, the imperial house was in decline and chaos reigned across the land. In the city of Zhuo Commandery, three men met: a straw-sandal weaver and mat-seller, a wine-merchant and pig-butcher of rough-hewn temper, and a red-faced giant who had wandered the land as a fugitive. Behind Zhang Fei's cottage in a peach orchard, they burned incense and swore an oath: "We ask not to be born the same day, the same month, the same year — but we ask to die the same day, the same month, the same year." This single bow created the most stirring bond of brotherhood in all Chinese literature. The ancient Zhuo Commandery is today's Zhuozhou in Hebei. Within the old city, two Liao-dynasty brick pagodas — the Zhuozhou Twin Pagodas — stand facing each other north and south: one is the Zhidu Temple Pagoda, the other the Yunju Temple Pagoda, still standing after a thousand years of wind and rain. Below the twin pagodas, the old city's lanes wind in curves. Though the peach orchard where Liu, Guan, and Zhang swore their oath is long gone, strolling through these streets you can still feel that spirit of utter devotion — three ordinary men of humble birth, through trust and mutual support, carved out their own domain amid a turbulent world. The Sanyi Temple southwest of Zhuozhou, first built in the Sui-Tang period and restored through successive dynasties, houses statues of the three sworn brothers — their bond has been worshipped by countless generations. Liu Bei, though a "mat-weaver and sandal-seller," harbored great ambitions; Guan Yu, "a fugitive who fled to Zhuo Commandery" after killing a man in a righteous cause, wandered the land; Zhang Fei, "a man of considerable property," sold wine and butchered pigs but eagerly befriended heroes from everywhere — three men of vastly different backgrounds met and knew one another in troubled times. That one bow surpassed mere martial alliance. The Peach Garden Oath defined the highest ideal of "brotherhood" in the Chinese heart — "to serve the state above and give peace to the people below" — and branded the character of "righteousness" deep into the bloodstream of Chinese culture. The twin pagodas stand silent, enduring through the centuries, as if still guarding the covenant of that long-vanished orchard.

stops.title: Stop Two: Hulao Pass and Guandu · Contending Powers Vie for Supremacy
stops.content: After the three Peach Garden brothers joined the coalition against Dong Zhuo, they performed the classic feat of "Three Heroes Against Lü Bu" before Hulao Pass. But what truly established Cao Cao's hegemony over the north was the Battle of Guandu in the fifth year of Jian'an (200 AD) — Cao Cao crushed Yuan Shao's hundred-thousand-strong army with a mere twenty thousand troops, burning the Wuchao granaries and deciding the fate of the realm in a single stroke. Hulao Pass has long since sunk into the old course of the Yellow River, but the ruins of the Eastern Han capital — the Han-Wei Luoyang Ancient City (including the Biyong Stele) — can still be explored today. This capital site, covering an area of one hundred square kilometers, witnessed the dying rays of the Eastern Han, the rise of Cao Wei, and the brief reunification of the Western Jin. Stand on these ruins and gaze eastward: the smoke and dust of the Guandu battlefield have long since dispersed, but Cao Cao's military genius — prevailing against overwhelming odds and turning the tide of history — still commands awe. And south of Luoyang, the Longmen Grottoes, a treasure-house of Buddhist art carved after the Northern Wei moved its capital to Luoyang — though the Three Kingdoms have long passed, Luoyang's status as "the center of the realm" has never changed. Hulao Pass connects the Songshan Mountains in the south with the Yellow River in the north, and was the strategic throat east of Luoyang since ancient times — the stage for "Three Heroes Against Lü Bu" in Romance of the Three Kingdoms. The legends of Guan Yu slaying Hua Xiong while his wine was still warm, and Zhang Fei's wild spear-duel with Lü Bu — though embellishments of the novelist's imagination — made Hulao one of the most vivid battlefields in the Three Kingdoms saga. Historically, when Yuan Shao and Cao Cao faced off at Guandu, the strategist Xu You, angered after Yuan Shao scolded him for a family offense, defected to Cao Cao overnight. When Cao Cao heard that Xu You had arrived, he "went out to greet him barefoot" — not even stopping to put on his shoes. Xu You proposed burning Yuan Shao's supply depot at Wuchao. Cao Cao personally led five thousand elite cavalry in a night raid on the granaries, setting fire to all of Yuan Shao's provisions in a single conflagration. "When the grain is gone, the army collapses" — the hundred-thousand-strong force dissolved overnight. This classic example of vanquishing a hundred thousand with twenty thousand remains a textbook case in world military history.

stops.title: Stop Three: Red Cliffs · The Easterly Wind that Favored Zhou Yu
stops.content: In the thirteenth year of Jian'an (208 AD), Cao Cao led over two hundred thousand troops south, intending to sweep away the forces south of the Yangtze in a single campaign. The allied armies of Sun Quan and Liu Bei prepared a fire attack at Red Cliffs. Zhou Yu and Zhuge Liang joined forces, borrowed an easterly wind overnight, and set fire to Cao Cao's fleet — "in the midst of laughter and talk, the masts and oars turned to flying ash." This battle decisively shattered Cao Cao's dream of unifying the empire and established the tripartite balance of power. The Red Cliffs rise from the southern bank of the Yangtze. The two characters "赤壁" (Red Cliffs) carved into the cliff face remain legible after a thousand years of wind and rain — this is the Red Cliffs Cliff Inscriptions. Standing atop the cliffs and looking out over the Yangtze as it surges eastward, you can almost see the towering fires of that fateful night. Countless scholars and poets of later ages have left their inscriptions here in remembrance, each character a meditation on that earth-shaking battle. The river wind whistles past, as if carrying Zhou Yu's commands and the war cries of the soldiers — it was an age of heroes, and every man wrote his own legend with his life. The great drama directed jointly by Zhou Yu and Zhuge Liang unfolded link by link: first, Huang Gai presented the "ruse of the battered body," receiving a public flogging from Zhou Yu to convince Cao Cao that his defection was genuine; then Pang Tong presented the "chain-link ruse," advising Cao Cao to bind his ships stem to stern with iron chains to reduce the rocking of the waves — unwittingly playing into the fire attack. Before the battle, Cao Cao, balancing his spear and chanting a poem, recited his "Short Song Ballad" — "The moon is bright, the stars are few; crows fly southward" — confident that the empire was as good as his. Who could have known that the easterly wind would suddenly rise, that Huang Gai's fire ships would race like arrows into Cao Cao's fleet, that the flames would spread from mid-river to the camps on shore, and that Cao Cao would flee north in desperate haste? Su Shi would write centuries later: "The great river flows east, washing away all the gallant heroes of a thousand ages" — the river wind that blew that night still carried the scorched smell of Red Cliffs when it reached Su Shi three hundred years later.

stops.title: Stop Four: Jingzhou · The Loss of Jingzhou Through Carelessness
stops.content: After the Battle of Red Cliffs, Liu Bei borrowed Jingzhou as a base of operations, and Guan Yu held it for ten years. Jingzhou lay at the heart of the realm — controlling the Han and Mian rivers to the north, commanding the trade of the Southern Seas to the south, connecting to Wu and Kuaiji in the east, and linking to Ba and Shu in the west — Zhuge Liang had already pointed out its strategic importance in his "Longzhong Strategy." But in the twenty-fourth year of Jian'an (219 AD), while Guan Yu was on campaign against Xiangyang and Fan, his rear lay exposed. Lü Meng's Wu forces, disguised as merchants in white robes, crossed the Yangtze and seized Jingzhou by stealth — "the loss of Jingzhou through carelessness" became an eternal regret. Today's Jingzhou City Wall, though rebuilt in the Ming and Qing dynasties, remains imposing — eleven kilometers in circumference, with six majestic gates. Mounting the gate tower, you stand on the very ground Guan Yu once defended; the Yangtze rolls eastward in the distance. Among the wall's brick and stone, arrow embrasures and hidden military chambers are still visible — the reputation of "the perfect fortress of the south" is well deserved. This wall has seen too much: it witnessed Guan Yu's inundation of the Seven Armies that shook the realm, and it witnessed his desperate retreat to Maicheng. A hero's last stand — nothing wrings the heart more. The struggle for Jingzhou was the most complex game between Wu and Shu. After Red Cliffs, Liu Bei "borrowed" Jingzhou from Sun Quan to establish a foothold, and Eastern Wu resented the arrangement bitterly. Lu Su once met Guan Yu alone, sword in hand, to negotiate its return, but Guan Yu refused to yield. During Guan Yu's tenure in Jingzhou, his "inundation of the Seven Armies" captured Yu Jin and killed Pang De — it was the most glorious moment of his life. But glory cannot last forever. Lü Meng's Wu forces, "all dressed in white robes, rowing as merchants," launched a surprise attack that captured Jingzhou behind Guan Yu's back. Gong'an, Nan Commandery, Jiangling, Yiling — city after city fell into Wu hands. Guan Yu was forced to flee westward to Maicheng, where he was captured and killed at Linju. Standing on Jingzhou's city wall and looking south, you can almost see that red-faced, long-bearded figure riding away — the fall of a city often begins with a single word: pride.

stops.title: Stop Five: White Emperor Town · The Dying Ruler's Entrustment
stops.content: In the second year of Zhangwu (222 AD), Liu Bei raised the full force of Shu to avenge Guan Yu, but was defeated at Yiling by Lu Xun, who burned seven hundred li of his interconnected camps. Liu Bei retreated in desperation to White Emperor Town. The following year, he fell gravely ill there. On his deathbed, he entrusted his heir Liu Shan to Zhuge Liang: "Your talent is ten times that of Cao Pi, and you will surely stabilize the state and accomplish the great enterprise. If my successor can be assisted, assist him. If he proves unworthy, you may take the realm yourself." Zhuge Liang knelt, weeping: "I shall exhaust the strength of my limbs, serve with utmost loyalty, and follow you in death!" White Emperor Town perches on White Emperor Mountain at the mouth of Qutang Gorge, protected by water on three sides in a position of formidable natural strength. Within the White Emperor Temple, the Hall of Bright Virtue, the Temple of Marquis Wu, and the Star-Gazing Pavilion still survive, along with over eighty stelae from successive dynasties. Standing at White Emperor Town and gazing toward Kuimen Gate, where the Yangtze bursts through the mountains with breathtaking force — "Leaving White Emperor Town in the morning amid colored clouds, I return to Jiangling in a single day" — the exhilaration of Li Bai's verse and the tragedy of Liu Bei's dying entrustment overlap under the same sky. The wind howls through the gorge like weeping, as if telling the story of that heart-wrenching night eighteen centuries ago. The Battle of Yiling was another classic fire attack — Lu Xun waited at ease for the Shu army's energy to deplete in the dense forests of Yiling. It was high summer; Liu Bei's seven hundred li of interconnected camp stockades left a fatal vulnerability that Lu Xun keenly grasped: "When an army first assembles, its thinking is concentrated and precise — one should not challenge it. Now that they have been here long, they have gained no advantage. Their soldiers are weary and their spirits flagging — to attack at their flank: this is the moment." In a single night, fire fed by wind and wind driven by flame consumed over forty of Shu's camp stockades. After Liu Bei withdrew to White Emperor Town, Zhuge Liang hurried from Chengdu. "Had Fa Zheng been alive, we would never have come to this" — those words were filled with regret and lament. The remains of the Eight Battle Array below White Emperor Town are said to be where Zhuge Liang drilled his troops. Du Fu wrote: "His achievement overshadowed the tripartite realm, his fame was sealed by the Eight Battle Arrays. The river flows, but the stones remain fixed — the lasting regret is the failure to swallow Wu." The river surges on for a thousand years; the stones of the Eight Battle Arrays are long gone. But the regret still moves every heart that stands on White Emperor Mountain.

stops.title: Stop Six: Chengdu's Temple of Marquis Wu · Utmost Loyalty unto Death
stops.content: Zhuge Liang, entrusted with the weight of Liu Bei's dying command, assisted the young ruler Liu Shan. He allied with Eastern Wu externally, cultivated good governance internally, crossed the Lu River in the fifth month, penetrated the barbarous lands, captured and released Meng Huo seven times to pacify the south. From the sixth to the twelfth year of Jianxing, he launched five northern expeditions and six campaigns from Mount Qi — until the autumn wind on Wuzhang Plains consumed the last drop of oil from the lamp of his life. "Before his expedition could succeed, he died — a thing that ever makes heroes weep." The Chengdu Temple of Marquis Wu is China's only temple dedicated jointly to a ruler and his minister. The Hall of Liu Bei and the Hall of Zhuge Liang stand linked front to back, while the Huiling Mausoleum rests quietly to one side. Ancient cypresses tower within the temple grounds; red walls line the walkways. The stone tablets bearing Yue Fei's hand-copied "Memorials on the Expedition" before and after inspire profound reverence. Around the Qingming Festival each year, Chengdu residents come here on pilgrimages and to pay homage to the "old minister who served two reigns with all his heart." Standing before Zhuge Liang's hall, gazing at his statue with feather fan and scholar's cap, you feel — he has long been more than a historical figure; he is the embodiment of wisdom and the symbol of loyalty in the Chinese heart. Inside the main gate, to the left, stands the "Stele of Three Perfections" — composed by the Tang-dynasty prime minister Pei Du, written by the calligrapher Liu Gongchuo, and carved by the master craftsman Lu Jian — the three perfections of composition, calligraphy, and engraving united, echoing the "perfection of wisdom" attributed to Zhuge Liang himself. Also within the temple are the stone tablets of Yue Fei's hand-copied "Memorials on the Expedition": "I was once a commoner, farming in Nanyang" — the brushstrokes, vigorous as sword blades, are said to have been dashed off by Yue Fei when he stayed overnight at the temple, so stirred was he by Zhuge Liang's passionate words. Huiling — the burial mound of Liu Bei — rests within the temple grounds, the tumulus about twelve meters high, covered in towering verdant cypresses. The emperor and his prime minister have shared incense offerings in the same temple for over seventeen hundred years. In spring, with the ginkgo trees a brilliant gold and the red walls framing the green, the scene of "the dense cypress grove outside Jinguan City" is precisely what Du Fu saw thirteen centuries ago.

stops.title: Stop Seven: Wuzhang Plains and Dingjun Mountain · The Star Falls in the Autumn Wind
stops.content: In autumn of the twelfth year of Jianxing (234 AD), Zhuge Liang's army was encamped on the Wuzhang Plains, confronting Sima Yi across the Wei River. The northern expedition had reached its most critical phase — but Zhuge Liang, worn out by years of overwork, could hold on no longer. That night, a great star streaked from northeast to southwest and fell over the encampment. The Marquis who had given his utmost loyalty unto death had finished his magnificent yet heartbreaking life. "The dead Zhuge scares away the living Zhongda" — even in death he laid one last empty-city ruse to prevent Sima Yi from pursuing. Zhuge Liang's dying wish was to be buried at Dingjun Mountain in Hanzhong — this is today's Tomb of Marquis Wu. The tomb garden is filled with ancient cypresses; the halls are solemn. The burial mound rests quietly in the embrace of green Dingjun Mountain. The Mian County Temple of Marquis Wu, built in the sixth year of Jingyao (263 AD), is one of the earliest temples dedicated to Zhuge Liang in the country. The autumn wind rises again. Standing on Dingjun Mountain and looking into the distance, the Wei River lies like a ribbon, the Qinling Mountains like a screen — the figure in the feather fan and scholar's cap has become an eternal legend woven into this landscape. The Wuzhang Plains are a loess plateau about one hundred and fifty meters high, leaning against the Qinling Mountains to the south and facing the Wei River to the north — an impregnable position. Zhuge Liang chose this place to camp precisely in order to control the route from Guanzhong into Hanzhong. He invented the wooden ox and flowing horse for mountain transport, improved the repeating crossbow to fire ten bolts at once, and deployed the Eight Trigrams Battle Array to confuse his enemies. Yet Sima Yi's judgment — "He eats little but concerns himself with many matters — how can he last long?" — became a fatal prophecy. In his final moments, Zhuge Liang was still arranging the retreat: "After I die, you may withdraw to Hanzhong. Jiang Wei shall bring up the rear, with Wei Yan as his deputy." He transmitted all the military knowledge of his lifetime to Jiang Wei, and begged Yang Yi to "never abandon fairness in public discourse" — even at the moment of death, his heart was with the safety of Shu Han, not his own life. That falling general's star became the morning star over Dingjun Mountain — every dawn, it still shines above the Tomb of Marquis Wu. The autumn wind on Wuzhang Plains — the hero's tears fell into the Wei River, and have never dried.
